claim: The Committee's criterion (ii) says My Son is 'an exceptional example of cultural interchange, with an indigenous society adapting to external cultural influences, notably the Hindu art and architecture of the Indian sub-continent'.

evidence.quote: Criterion (ii): The My Son Sanctuary is an exceptional example of cultural interchange, with an indigenous society adapting to external cultural influences, notably the Hindu art and architecture of the Indian sub-continent.

The My Son Sanctuary is an exceptional example of cultural interchange, with an indigenous society adapting to external cultural influences, notably the Hindu art and architecture of the Indian sub-continent.

claim: The advisory body ICOMOS had recommended different words for criterion (ii): 'with the introduction the Hindu architecture of the Indian sub-continent into South-East Asia'. The Committee replaced them with 'an indigenous society adapting to external cultural influences'.

evidence.quote: Criterion ii The My Son Sanctuary is an exceptional example of cultural interchange, with the introduction the Hindu architecture of the Indian sub-continent into South-East Asia.
with an indigenous society adapting to external cultural influences

claim: UNESCO's own summary: a culture on the coast of Vietnam 'owed its spiritual origins to the Hinduism of the Indian sub-continent'; many temples were built to Hindu divinities 'such as Krishna and Vishnu, but above all Shiva'; and 'Shivite Hinduism remained the established state religion'.

evidence.quote: Under this influence many temples were built to the Hindu divinities such as Krishna and Vishnu, but above all Shiva.
Shivite Hinduism remained the established state religion.
but above all Shiva.

notes: 'Hindu' is UNESCO's and ICOMOS's word for the Cham royal Shaiva cult; the inscriptions themselves speak of Shiva, Bhadresvara, Isanesvara etc. Voice: say 'Shiva temples' or 'Hindu temples, as UNESCO calls them'.

claim: ICOMOS: the Cham came under the influence of the Hindu religion of the Indian sub-continent 'early in their development, though the exact date is not known'.

evidence.quote: The Cham came under the influence of the Hindu religion of the Indian sub-continent early in their development, though the exact date is not known.

notes: The honest 'how and when' answer: no source opened gives the date or the route. The nomination dossier (S04) also says the exact date is not known and that many dates 'are still open questions for historians'.

claim: The first temple, built by Bhadravarman, was burned during the reign of Rudravarman I and rebuilt by Rudravarman's son Cambhuvarman, who gave the god the new name Cambhubhadresvara.

evidence.quote: reconstruit par le fils el SuCCesseur de ce roi Cambhuvarman, sous le nom de Cambhubhadrecvara
evidence.translation: It was rebuilt by the son and successor of this king, Cambhuvarman, under the name of Cambhubhadresvara.

evidence.locator: B 2.3, Stele of Cambhuvarman at My Son (BEFEO 15, p. 5)
evidence.quote: Restauration du temple de Bhadreçvara par Çanibhuvarman (première moitié du VIe siècle çaka), qui lui donne le nom de Çambhubhadreçvara.
evidence.translation: Restoration of the temple of Bhadresvara by Cambhuvarman (first half of the 6th century Saka), who gives it the name Cambhubhadresvara.

evidence.quote: was burnt by fire.

notes: 'Burned' rests on Cambhuvarman's own stele (Finot 1904: 'Cambhuvarman declares that they burned'). Saka 500-549 = about 578-627 CE for the rebuild; Majumdar puts Rudravarman I at 479-577 AD (hedged). Don't state a year.

claim: Nothing of Bhadravarman's original temple survives, and it was probably wooden: Finot wrote that nothing is left of it, 'probably of wood, since Cambhuvarman declares that they burned'. The Viet Nam dossier also says Bhadravarman built 'a wooden temple'.

evidence.translation: Of Bhadravarman's earliest buildings nothing remains; they were no doubt of wood, since Cambhuvarman declares that they burned.

evidence.quote: king Bhadravarman selected the MY SON valley to build a wooden temple to worship the Genius king.

notes: 'No doubt of wood' is Finot's inference; the dossier repeats it. Hedge: 'probably wooden'.

claim: In 875 CE (Saka 797) the Cham king Jaya Indravarman recorded on one stele both a Buddhist temple and monastery at Dong Duong (Lakshmindra Lokesvara) and his work on Shiva's lingam Bhadresvara at My Son, about 20 km apart.

evidence.quote: Elle porte la date de 797 caka — 875 À. D. et le nom du roi Jaya Indravarman
evidence.translation: It bears the date 797 Saka = 875 AD and the name of king Jaya Indravarman

evidence.quote: est la fondation d'un temple et d'un monastère
evidence.translation: the proper object of the act is the foundation of a Buddhist temple and monastery dedicated to Lakshmindra Lokesvara

evidence.quote: on comprend qu'Indravarman ait rappelé ses deux fondations par une même inscription
evidence.translation: one understands that Indravarman recalled his two foundations in a single inscription

evidence.translation: who must have limited himself to re-erecting the lingam

One edition only (1904); the ISAW corpus has not published this stele. Fresh angle F2. 'About 20 km' is Finot's figure ('20 kilomêtres').

claim: The same 875 stele tells a legend in place of the history: Bhrigu is sent from heaven by Maheshvara and sets up the Bhadresvara lingam at Champa, and Uroja descends to rule; Finot notes the author 'completely ignores' the real founders Bhadravarman and Cambhuvarman.

evidence.quote: Ces faits sont complètement ignorés de l'auteur de notre inscription

evidence.translation: Since then Bhadresvara has been the great protector of the kingdom of Champa.

notes: Shows how the story of the founder grew: a king of the 4th-5th century (stele at My Son) became a god-sent figure by 875. Finot is the only reader; ISAW has not republished.

claim: Among the 130 Champa inscriptions in Majumdar's 1927 collection, he counts 92 for Shiva and the gods linked to him, 3 for Vishnu, 5 for Brahma and 7 for the Buddha.

claim: Louis Finot (1915) read the Vo-canh inscription, the best-known early Sanskrit text of Champa (found in Khanh Hoa province, not at My Son), as Buddhist in inspiration; it names a king 'descendant of Sri Mara'.
